chapter: Young players, Coltrane and the avant-garde
title: Young black musicians losing interest; the all-black band problem
summary: Sam is bothered that black players skip rehearsal while white players show up, and says Thad Jones faced the same.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Let me say this--it's another thing that I'm sad about, uh, uh, it's kind of hard to say, but I think it's necessary to be said. Our black young kids, they's always finding a way to get over, or get around the truth. Now, they don't never want to come seem to me it's hard to get a group of young black kids to come to learn something about this culture, man. But, you mention something to a group of white kids, man, and you, and you can't find room for them, you know, 'cause

they coming in by mobs, you know. And that bothers me very, it bothers me very much. Uh, that those that that are out here on the scene, they, it's something, it's it's a question mark over over my head, and I want to find out--I'd like to--

--when I put my band together, um, I wanted all-black band because I figured these guys, I get these guys all-black band then, uh, I could uh, explain uh, what kind of, what kind of uh, feeling, what kind of--where I wanted to phrase them. So when I put this, I went to say to the musicians--I won't call any names, fine, yeah, man, just let me know, just let me know what uh, when you're going to have rehearsal. So, OK, now I'm ready, got my music together, got my book ready to go, uh, so I go to these people, and say, OK, man, you coming to rehearsal. Oh, man, uh, I can't make it to rehearsal, you know. So, I go to the, I say finish, go ahead. I go ahead to a white musicians head, man, can you come to rehearsal? Uh, I'm starting a band. Where, and when and what time, and he's there on the spot man, with his horn out ready to play. Now this been bugging me and this uh, not only me, uh this is probably why Thad Jones is not here today to front his band. Because Thad used to come in here man, and sit down in here, and, boy, we talk for hours about that. Even said, even turned around and give the downbeat
to the band, when he turned around to the band; face the band, he see all white folks. What happened to the dudes that he had, that he, you know--

And, and and it's very confusing, confusion man. Because uh, it it it's telling me and it's telling him, that the black musicians, man they they what is it, they losing interest in this art, you know. There's a lot of money that can be made playing the true art; classic jazz music, I know, I know because ...home here, I don't play nothing but jazz music, man. I, I mean, it ain't much, but it's OK for me, you know. I got a couple machines in the yard out there...you know what I mean, I ain't doing to bad, you know what I mean, I can eat, I can pay my bills, like telephone, you know what I mean, I got a few bucks down there in the bank, you know, but it ain't much. But, uh, it don't for me take much, you know. I don't want to live lavishly, you know, great big house and servants and all that kind of stuff, chauffeurs and that stuff, you see because, uh, all to get back to the thing, I think that I were a young jazz players is losing interest. They're trying to find a way to get over, and then when they do come, man, they, when you do have them in your band, then they half do the job, you know, they can't, they can't play the part that's given to them to play.
